questions.question_text: Under Virginia's Residential Property Disclosure Act, what must the seller of residential property provide to the buyer?
questions.correct_answer: A buyer-beware statement saying the owner makes no representations about the property
distractors: A detailed written list of all known material defects
A one-year warranty covering the property's condition
A certified appraisal of the property's market value
questions.explanation: Virginia uses a buyer-beware approach under the Residential Property Disclosure Act (Va. Code § 55.1-703). The seller furnishes a single standardized disclosure statement saying the owner makes no representations or warranties about the property's condition and that the buyer should exercise due diligence, such as a home inspection, before settlement. It is not a defect-disclosure form like those required in many other states.

questions.question_text: A Virginia seller knows the basement floods but provides the standard buyer-beware disclosure statement. Under Virginia's caveat emptor approach, what is the seller's duty regarding the flooding?
questions.correct_answer: The seller need not volunteer it but cannot conceal it or lie if asked
distractors: The seller must affirmatively disclose it in the statement
The seller has no duty even if the buyer asks directly
The seller must disclose it only after the home inspection
questions.explanation: Virginia follows caveat emptor (Va. Code § 55.1-703). A seller using the buyer-beware disclosure statement is generally not required to volunteer known defects, but the seller may not actively conceal a defect, divert the buyer from discovering it, or lie in response to a direct question. So the seller need not list the flooding but cannot hide it or misrepresent it if asked.

questions.question_text: When must the Virginia residential property disclosure statement be delivered to the buyer?
questions.correct_answer: Before or at contract ratification
distractors: Within 10 days of listing the property
At the home inspection appointment
At the closing table only
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-708 requires the owner to deliver the disclosure statement to the purchaser prior to ratification of the real estate purchase contract. Late delivery gives the purchaser a right to terminate under § 55.1-709.

questions.question_text: A Virginia buyer is hand-delivered the residential property disclosure statement two days after contract ratification. How long does the buyer have to terminate the contract?
questions.correct_answer: 3 days from hand delivery
distractors: 5 days from hand delivery
7 calendar days from hand delivery
No right to terminate after ratification
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-709 gives the purchaser three days to terminate if the statement is hand delivered or delivered by electronic means, or five days if it is sent by U.S. mail. The right ends earlier at settlement, occupancy, the buyer's loan application, or a written waiver.

questions.question_text: What does the standard Virginia residential property disclosure statement tell buyers about the property's condition?
questions.correct_answer: The owner makes no representations and the buyer should exercise due diligence
distractors: The owner certifies all major systems are functional
The owner warrants the property is free of defects
The owner guarantees clear title to the property
questions.explanation: Virginia's Residential Property Disclosure Act (Va. Code § 55.1-703) uses a single buyer-beware statement. It tells the purchaser that the owner makes no representations or warranties about the condition of the property and that the buyer should exercise whatever due diligence they deem necessary, such as obtaining a home inspection, before settlement.

questions.question_text: The Chesapeake Bay Preservation Act primarily affects properties in which part of Virginia?
questions.correct_answer: Eastern Virginia near tidal waters
distractors: Western mountain regions only
All counties statewide equally
Properties along the James River only
questions.explanation: The Chesapeake Bay Preservation Act applies to Tidewater localities in eastern Virginia within the Bay watershed, which must designate Resource Protection Areas and Resource Management Areas to protect water quality. Va. Code § 55.1-703 tells purchasers to exercise due diligence about whether a property sits in one.

questions.question_text: A buyer is interested in a waterfront lot in eastern Virginia. The agent discovers the lot includes a 100-foot Resource Protection Area. What must be disclosed?
questions.correct_answer: The property is within an RPA zone
distractors: Nothing if the seller chose no representations
Only that a survey is recommended
Only if the buyer plans to build
questions.explanation: A known Resource Protection Area is a material fact about the property that a licensee with actual knowledge must disclose (Va. Code § 54.1-2131/2132), and § 55.1-703 directs purchasers to investigate Chesapeake Bay resource protection areas. RPAs include a 100-foot buffer around tidal and certain non-tidal wetlands, which sharply limits land disturbance.

questions.question_text: A home near Naval Air Station Oceana in Virginia Beach is listed for sale. What special disclosure may be required?
questions.correct_answer: Military noise and accident potential zones
distractors: Federal security clearance requirements
Restricted airspace navigation rules
Naval housing priority purchase rights
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-704 requires the owner of residential property in a locality with a military air installation to disclose whether the property is in a noise zone or accident potential zone designated by the locality's ordinance, and the zone designation. Effective July 1, 2025, HB 1706/SB 1210 also added public-use airport noise to the due-diligence items in § 55.1-703.

questions.question_text: What is the width of the vegetated buffer required in a Chesapeake Bay Resource Protection Area?
questions.correct_answer: 100 feet
distractors: 50 feet
75 feet
200 feet
questions.explanation: Chesapeake Bay Preservation Area regulations require a 100-foot vegetated buffer landward of tidal shores, tidal wetlands, and connected non-tidal wetlands. The buffer limits land disturbance and filters pollutants before runoff reaches the Bay.

questions.question_text: A property is located in a Resource Management Area but NOT in a Resource Protection Area. Which statement is correct?
questions.correct_answer: Development is allowed with best practices
distractors: No development is permitted at all
The same rules as RPAs apply
RMA designation has no effect
questions.explanation: Resource Management Areas (RMAs) allow development but require best management practices to minimize environmental impact. They are less restrictive than RPAs, which impose stricter buffer and development limitations.

questions.question_text: A murder occurred in a Virginia home five years ago. Must the listing agent disclose this to prospective buyers?
questions.correct_answer: No, stigmatized events are not material defects
distractors: Yes, all deaths must be disclosed
Only if the buyer asks in writing
Yes, within the first 10 years
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-713 A bars any cause of action against an owner or a real estate licensee for failing to disclose that a property was the site of a homicide, felony, or suicide, or of any act or occurrence that had no effect on the physical structure, its physical environment, or the improvements. There is no duty to volunteer stigmatizing events.

questions.question_text: A buyer asks a Virginia agent whether any registered sex offenders live near a listed property. What is the agent's obligation?
questions.correct_answer: Inform the buyer the registry is public
distractors: Search the registry and provide names
Disclose all offenders within one mile
State that no offenders live nearby
questions.explanation: Virginia does not require a licensee to research or disclose sex offender information. Va. Code § 55.1-703 directs purchasers to exercise due diligence using the Virginia Sex Offender and Crimes Against Minors Registry, and the licensee should point the buyer to that public resource rather than answering for it.

questions.question_text: A Virginia home is served by an onsite sewage system whose operating permit was issued with a waiver. What must the owner disclose to a purchaser?
questions.correct_answer: That the waiver becomes void upon transfer of the property
distractors: The full maintenance history of the system
Nothing, because the system is functioning
The results of a new septic inspection
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 32.1-164.1:1 requires the owner to give the purchaser a written disclosure, prior to acceptance of the purchase contract, that any operating permit granted a waiver is null and void at the time of transfer or sale. Virginia's Residential Property Disclosure Act itself is buyer-beware — § 55.1-703 only tells purchasers to exercise due diligence about the wastewater system and septic maintenance.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is considered a stigmatized property condition in Virginia that does NOT require disclosure?
questions.correct_answer: A suicide occurred in the home
distractors: A failing septic system on the lot
Known flooding in the basement
Active termite infestation damage
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-713 A shields owners and licensees from liability for not disclosing that a property was the site of a homicide, felony, or suicide, or an act with no effect on the physical structure. Failing septic, flooding, and termite damage are material adverse facts about the physical condition that a licensee with actual knowledge must disclose under § 54.1-2131 B.

questions.question_text: A seller's home was the site of a drug-related felony arrest. Under Virginia law, is this a material defect?
questions.correct_answer: No, felonies are stigmatized conditions
distractors: Yes, all criminal activity must be disclosed
Only if the felony involved violence
Only within 3 years of the event
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-713 A specifically lists a felony among the events that create no cause of action for nondisclosure. Neither the owner nor the licensee has a duty to volunteer it.

questions.question_text: Under the Virginia Resale Disclosure Act, if the purchase contract specifies no review period, how long does a buyer have to cancel after receiving the resale certificate?
questions.correct_answer: 3 days
distractors: 5 days
7 days
10 days
questions.explanation: Since July 1, 2025 the Virginia Resale Disclosure Act (Va. Code § 55.1-2307 et seq.) governs both condominium and property owners' association resales with a single resale certificate. Under § 55.1-2312 the parties may set the review period in the contract; if they do not, the purchaser has three days from receipt of the certificate — or from notice that it is unavailable — to cancel.

questions.question_text: A seller requests the resale certificate for a home in a property owners' association. How long does the association have to deliver it?
questions.correct_answer: 14 days from the request
distractors: 7 days from the request
30 days from the request
5 business days from the request
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-2309 requires the association, its managing agent, or the third party preparing the certificate to deliver it within 14 days after a written request by the seller or the seller's agent. If nothing is delivered in that window the resale certificate is deemed unavailable, which starts the purchaser's cancellation clock.

questions.question_text: Which item is included in a Virginia resale certificate?
questions.correct_answer: Current assessments, fees, and reserve funds
distractors: The original developer's profit margins
Individual owner financial statements
Adjacent property tax assessments
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-2310 lists roughly 30 required contents, including current assessments and fees, the association's financial statements and reserve information, pending litigation, governing documents and rules, insurance information (including whether an owner may owe part of the master policy deductible), and restrictions on flags, solar devices, signs, parking, home businesses, and rentals.

questions.question_text: An association charges a fee to prepare a resale certificate. How is that fee regulated in Virginia?
questions.correct_answer: The Common Interest Community Board sets the maximum allowable fees
distractors: Any fee is allowed as long as it is reasonable
Resale certificates must be provided free of charge
The fee is capped at $100 by statute
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 55.1-2316 provides that the Common Interest Community Board establishes the maximum fees an association or its agent may charge for preparing, updating, expediting, and delivering a resale certificate, and requires those maximums to be adjusted for inflation using the CPI-U at least every five years. The fees are capped by Board schedule, not left to the association's judgment.

questions.question_text: A condo resale certificate reveals the association is involved in active litigation. How does this affect the buyer?
questions.correct_answer: The buyer can cancel within the review period
distractors: The sale is automatically voided
The buyer must accept the risk
Litigation voids the resale certificate
questions.explanation: Pending litigation is a required disclosure in the resale certificate under Va. Code § 55.1-2310. If the risk is unacceptable, the purchaser may cancel within the review period set in the contract or, if none is set, within three days of receipt under § 55.1-2312.

questions.question_text: A Virginia agent cold-calls a prospect who is on the National Do-Not-Call Registry. What has the agent violated?
questions.correct_answer: Federal and state Do-Not-Call laws
distractors: Only state telemarketing regulations
No law if calling about real estate
Only REALTOR association ethics rules
questions.explanation: Real estate solicitation calls are covered by the federal Telephone Consumer Protection Act rules and by the Virginia Telephone Privacy Protection Act (Va. Code § 59.1-510 et seq.), which incorporates the national registry. Licensees must scrub against the registry before making unsolicited calls.

questions.question_text: After a listing presentation, what should a Virginia agent leave with the property owner?
questions.correct_answer: Copies of all signed documents
distractors: Only a business card
Nothing until the property sells
A verbal summary of the agreement
questions.explanation: 18VAC135-20-310 requires licensees to deliver copies of any written instrument promptly after execution and to leave copies with the appropriate parties, so the owner keeps a record of everything signed at the listing presentation.

questions.question_text: A consumer asks a Virginia agent about avoiding telemarketing calls. What should the agent disclose?
questions.correct_answer: The Do-Not-Call registry is available
distractors: There is no way to stop solicitations
Only the state registry exists
Call blocking is the only option
questions.explanation: The National Do-Not-Call Registry is free and open to consumers, and Virginia's Telephone Privacy Protection Act (Va. Code § 59.1-510 et seq.) works from the same registry. Pointing consumers to it is both accurate and good practice.

questions.question_text: Agent Martinez receives a signed buyer agency agreement. When must a copy be provided to the buyer?
questions.correct_answer: At the time of signing
distractors: Within 5 business days
At closing only
Only if the buyer requests one
questions.explanation: 18VAC135-20-310 requires prompt delivery of copies of executed instruments to the parties. Handing the buyer a copy at signing satisfies that duty; sitting on it does not.

questions.question_text: Which best describes a Virginia licensee's obligation regarding due diligence in a transaction?
questions.correct_answer: Exercise reasonable care throughout
distractors: Guarantee a successful closing
Only verify what the seller discloses
Perform a full property inspection
questions.explanation: Va. Code § 54.1-2131 and § 54.1-2132 require a licensee to exercise ordinary care throughout the transaction — timely presentation of offers, required disclosures, proper document delivery, and accounting for funds.
